prompt: How would you onboard a new engineer onto your team?
answer_markdown: Answer with a concrete shape, not a documentation wish-list. The single highest-value decision is the first task: small, real, and shippable within about three days. Not a toy, because toys teach nothing about your actual systems, and not a large project, because a new hire needs to complete the full loop — write, review, merge, deploy, observe — before they need to hold a big architecture in their head. Shipping on day three beats understanding the architecture in week three. Pair with them on it rather than assigning it, because what you are really transmitting is the invisible layer: which channel to ask in, which test suite is flaky, who owns which service, why that module has a 'do not touch' comment. None of that is written down anywhere and discovering it alone costs weeks. Have them fix documentation gaps as they hit them, since they are the only person who can currently see what is missing — in two months they will have the same blindness as everyone else. Then escalate: own a small feature by week two, review someone else's PR and shadow on-call by week four, lead a small design discussion by week eight.

prompt: What's the difference between mentoring and sponsorship, and why does it matter?
answer_markdown: Mentoring is giving advice — answering questions, reviewing code, explaining how things work. Sponsorship is spending your own credibility on someone: putting their name forward for the visible project, letting them present the design review you could have presented, recommending them for the promotion. The distinction matters because mentoring is comfortable and costs you almost nothing, while sponsorship costs you something real, which is precisely why it is what actually changes careers. Advice helps someone get better at a job they already have; sponsorship gets them a bigger one. It is also the fairness dimension of the topic — sponsorship tends to flow toward people who resemble the sponsor, so doing it deliberately rather than by instinct matters. In an interview, recognising the distinction is a strong senior signal, and the best answers include a specific example of visible work you handed to someone who was not the obvious choice.

prompt: How do you know when to step in and when to let someone struggle?
answer_markdown: Calibrate on the cost of the mistake, not just the clock. Every intervention removes a lesson, so the question before jumping in is what this particular mistake actually costs. Let them ship the imperfect abstraction and refactor it in a month — the recovery is the learning and the kerb is cheap. Do not let them drop the production table, and intervene immediately on anything touching production data, security, or a customer commitment, regardless of how long they have been at it. Within the safe zone, a rough time-based ladder works: under 30 minutes, leave them alone because struggle is the learning; around an hour, ask what they have tried and hint at the area; around two hours, pair — but with their hands on the keyboard. That last detail carries the most weight, because the instinct when pairing with someone stuck is to take over and type, which is faster and feels helpful and guarantees they cannot do it next time. Past about four hours the cost of being blocked exceeds the value of the lesson, so unblock them directly.

prompt: You're mentoring someone who messages you five or six times a day with questions he could answer himself in fifteen minutes. Your own work is slipping and after three months he's asking the same kind of question. What do you do?
answer_markdown: Change the shape of the help rather than its volume, and say so explicitly so it does not read as a confusing withdrawal. Fast answers are a trap that feels like generosity: you have made yourself the shortest path to a solution, so he has never built the investigation muscle — you optimised for his comfort against his growth. But refusing outright is worse in a different direction, because it removes his support and teaches him not to ask. The move is: 'I have noticed I am answering things you could find, and I do not think that is helping you. Before you ask, spend fifteen minutes and tell me where you looked — I will point you at the right place rather than give the answer.' Then batch it into a standing thirty minutes a day, which cuts your interruptions and unexpectedly cuts his question count too, because roughly half resolve while he waits. One important exception: where he genuinely lacks context nobody could infer — team history, why a service exists, an undocumented decision — keep answering immediately. Making someone hunt for unknowable facts is not teaching.

prompt: A new hire six weeks in says 'all good' every standup, but her first PR has been open two weeks with no commits in five days. She's quiet in meetings. What do you do?
answer_markdown: Do not wait for her to ask for help, because the people least likely to ask are the ones who most need it, and reluctance tends to rise with how much someone feels they have to prove. 'Ask if you need anything' is a policy that systematically fails exactly the people it is meant to reach. Two weeks of a stalled PR is data — you already know. The key is to remove the need to ask rather than to interrogate: do not open with 'are you struggling?', which requires her to confess. Instead make help routine and non-diagnostic — 'I am going to grab thirty minutes on that PR with you, I want to look at the caching bit anyway.' Now she gets help without having requested it, and you find out what is actually wrong. While you are there, normalise your own confusion out loud; narrating 'I have never understood why this service does that, let me look it up' does more for someone's willingness to ask than any invitation ever will. Then fix the structural cause: if a PR can sit for two weeks unnoticed, that is a team problem, and a standing review rotation solves it for the next person too.

prompt: How do you mentor someone significantly more experienced than you?
answer_markdown: Separate expertise from context, which is the whole of this scenario. A twelve-year engineer joining your team is very likely a better engineer than you, and you know things about this system they cannot possibly know yet. Those two facts are not in conflict, and the framing that works says so explicitly: 'you know this pattern much better than I do — the thing I am worried about is specific to our provider. We hit their undocumented rate limit last March and it took a week to diagnose. Can I show you the incident doc?' Lead with evidence rather than authority, because you have none and claiming it is what makes this go badly. If they still disagree after seeing the evidence they may well be right, and you have done your job by making the information available rather than by winning. The reciprocal move is what makes this mentoring rather than a disagreement: your side of the exchange is transferring context, while you learn the pattern expertise from them. Interviewers ask this because people usually fail it in one of two directions — total deference to seniority, or overcorrecting into territorialism about 'their' codebase.
